candidates.attacker_control: An unauthenticated attacker can supply `logoutSuccessUrl` on a GET to the default logout endpoint; that parameter takes precedence over the configured logout URL. A request parameter supplied to the authentication-processing endpoint can control `spring-security-redirect` after successful login. The Referer header is also used as a fallback logout target.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: UrlUtils.isValidRedirectUrl exists, but it is not applied to either request-derived target; it is used for configured values, and its own check permits `http` URLs. RedirectUtils deliberately permits absolute HTTP(S) targets for configured redirects, so the callers must constrain request-supplied values. The request-parameter behavior is documented in LogoutFilter, which may indicate legacy intent, but it remains an unsafe trust decision. No runtime test or container redirect normalization was available.
candidates.impact: A trusted application origin can redirect a victim to an attacker-controlled external site, supporting phishing, credential harvesting, and redirection of authenticated users after login. This candidate does not by itself prove session theft or cross-origin code execution.
candidates.prerequisites: LogoutFilter or the default AuthenticationProcessingFilter target resolver must be enabled. For the post-login variant, `alwaysUseDefaultTargetUrl` must remain false (the default) and the victim must complete authentication with the attacker-supplied parameter present. A custom filter or external URL allow-list could prevent exploitation.
candidates.root_cause: Security UI redirect URLs are sourced directly from request parameters without verification that they resolve to the local application. LogoutFilter.determineTargetUrl() returns the `logoutSuccessUrl` request parameter (then the Referer header), and TargetUrlResolverImpl.determineTargetUrl() returns the decoded `spring-security-redirect` parameter. Both feed RedirectUtils, which treats any lowercase http:// or https:// value as an absolute destination and calls response.sendRedirect().
candidates.title: Unvalidated request-controlled redirect targets in logout and post-login flows
candidates.trace: LogoutFilter.doFilterHttp invokes handlers and then determineTargetUrl(); determineTargetUrl returns `request.getParameter("logoutSuccessUrl")` at lines 132-136 or `Referer` at 138-140. sendRedirect() delegates to RedirectUtils.sendRedirect() at line 161. For login, AbstractProcessingFilter.successfulAuthentication calls the configured TargetUrlResolver and then sends its result; TargetUrlResolverImpl returns the decoded request parameter at lines 61-66. RedirectUtils sees an absolute http(s) value at lines 38 and 56-58 and forwards it to response.sendRedirect at line 60.
candidates.unverified: Runtime confirmation is absent. It is unverified whether a particular application enables these default filters, whether a proxy or custom filter blocks external redirects, and how the target servlet container handles encodeRedirectURL for absolute external URLs.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-601: URL Redirection to Untrusted Site ('Open Redirect')

coverage_summary: The source scope reports 925 model-visible files. The P1 index parsed 627 Java files and 866 files total, with 59 source files omitted from the index; no SAST, data-flow, control-flow, or runtime analysis is available. I reviewed high-risk authentication, URL matching, redirect, SSL-channel, session, remember-me, ACL, CAS, OpenID, NTLM, pre-authentication, taglib, and representative sample flows. The repository contains no visible test tree, no dependencies were inspected, and I did not exhaustively read every one of the 925 files.
limitations: No code, tests, scanners, servlet container, or exploit payloads were executed; all conclusions are static source observations and unconfirmed leads.
The P1 relation index omits 59 files and provides no complete data-flow, semantic resolution, control-flow, reachability, or exploitability evidence.
Container behavior for sendRedirect, encodeRedirectURL, servletPath/pathInfo normalization, and HTTPS reverse-proxy handling could affect redirect and URL-matching exploitability.
Authentication/filter activation and URL allow-lists are deployment configuration and were not verified at runtime.
External library behavior (Spring LDAP, OpenID4Java, servlet container, JAAS login modules) was not inspected and remains a source of uncertainty.

rejected_leads.lead: Stored/reflected XSS in the generated login page via OpenID's raw last-username handling (openid/.../OpenIDAuthenticationProcessingFilter.java:98-103 and core/.../DefaultLoginPageGeneratingFilter.java:94-126)
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible missing output encoding, but exploitation depends on the optional generated login page plus a forced OpenID discovery/failure path. It was not selected as the single strongest source-evidenced candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Digest authentication replay because the client-supplied `uri` value, rather than the actual request URI, is used in the digest calculation (core/.../DigestProcessingFilter.java:133-137, 261-262 and 366-393)
rejected_leads.reason: The source shows missing URI-to-request binding, but the strongest impact requires capturing another user's Authorization header; protocol-wide replay limitations and runtime interposition are unverified.

rejected_leads.lead: Regex URL matcher may fail open when lowercase comparisons are requested because RegexUrlPathMatcher.compile does not lowercase the pattern while request URLs are lowercased
rejected_leads.reason: Source inconsistency is real, but exploitation requires a specific regex/configuration combination and no attacker-controlled reachability was proven.

rejected_leads.lead: Missing authorization checks in mutable ACL service mutation methods and possible JSR-250/interface annotation gaps
rejected_leads.reason: These require particular API exposure or proxy/interface configurations and were not traced to a concrete remote attack path.

summary: Static source review found one strongest candidate: request-controlled redirect targets in Spring Security's logout and post-login flows are passed to Servlet sendRedirect without same-origin or allow-list validation. LogoutFilter reads the `logoutSuccessUrl` request parameter (and Referer fallback), while TargetUrlResolverImpl reads `spring-security-redirect`; RedirectUtils accepts absolute HTTP(S) targets. This is a source-evidenced open-redirect lead, not runtime-confirmed. Other reviewed leads were rejected as more conditional or dependent on unverified container/runtime behavior.
